You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary at /workspace/dataset/test15_executable.
DO NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk anyway).
DO NOT use `strings`, `objdump`, `nm`, `gdb`, or any binary/symbol inspection. Behavioral probing via command-line arguments ONLY.

The binary's driver program is exactly this:

  inflection::Inflector::initialize();
  std::vector<std::string> results;
  for (int i = 1; i < argc && i <= 5; i++) {
      std::string word = argv[i];
      results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::pluralize(word));
      results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::camelize(word));
      if (i % 2 == 0) results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::underscore(word));
  }
  for (const auto& r : results) std::cout << r << std::endl;
  if (argc > 1) {
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::isPlural(argv[1]) << std::endl;
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::isSingular(argv[1]) << std::endl;
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::demodulize("Module::" + std::string(argv[1])) << std::endl;
  }

So to observe a function on an arbitrary word W:
  - pluralize(W)  -> line 1 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - camelize(W)   -> line 2 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - underscore(W) -> `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable dummy "W"` prints: pluralize(dummy), camelize(dummy), pluralize(W), camelize(W), underscore(W), then isPlural/isSingular/demodulize of "dummy". So underscore(W) is line 5.
  - isPlural(W)   -> line 3 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"` (prints as 0/1 since it's a bool via operator<<)
  - isSingular(W) -> line 4 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - demodulize("Module::" + W) -> line 5 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`

Run MANY probes (hundreds). Use bash loops. Quote arguments properly. Capture stderr too (2>&1 separately from stdout when it matters) and capture exit codes.
Be systematic: form a hypothesis, then design inputs that DISCRIMINATE between competing hypotheses, then confirm.
Report the exact rule as precise pseudocode operating on BYTES (the C++ code uses std::string = bytes; the "C" locale means std::toupper/tolower only affect ASCII a-z/A-Z). Explicitly test non-ASCII UTF-8 input to confirm byte-level behavior.


=== ADVERSARIAL CROSS-CHECK: demodulize ===

Another engineer probed the `demodulize` behavior of /workspace/dataset/test15_executable and produced this spec. Your job is to FALSIFY it. Assume it is subtly wrong. Design and run inputs specifically engineered to break it, then report every discrepancy between the spec's prediction and the binary's actual output.

SPEC PSEUDOCODE:
// inflection::Inflector::demodulize(const std::string& s)  -- BYTE-level spec
// CONFIRMED implementation is exactly:
//     size_t pos = s.rfind(':');          // last occurrence of the single BYTE 0x3A
//     return s.substr(pos + 2);           // throws std::out_of_range if pos+2 > s.size()
//
// Note the off-by-one: the intent was rfind("::") + 2 (== skip the two colons);
// the code searches for ONE colon but skips TWO bytes past it, so it always
// eats the last colon AND the byte immediately after it.

function demodulize(s: bytes) -> bytes:
    # 1. find index of the LAST byte equal to 0x3A (':')
    pos = -1
    for i in 0 .. len(s)-1:
        if s[i] == 0x3A: pos = i          # plain unsigned-byte equality; 0xBA etc. do NOT match
    # 2. no colon at all  -> std::string::rfind returns npos == SIZE_MAX (2^64-1);
    #    npos + 2 wraps to 1 (unsigned overflow), so the C++ code would evaluate s.substr(1).
    #    (Cannot be exercised through this driver: the driver always prepends "Module::".)
    if pos == -1:
        start = 1                          # inferred from unsigned wraparound, NOT observed
    else:
        start = pos + 2
    # 3. bounds check exactly like std::string::substr
    if start > len(s):
        THROW std::out_of_range(
          "basic_string::substr: __pos (which is " + start + ") > this->size() (which is " + len(s) + ")")
        # uncaught -> std::terminate -> abort (SIGABRT), process exit status 134 via shell
    # 4. byte slice to end of string, NO other transformation:
    #    no case change, no trimming, no UTF-8 awareness, no separator normalisation
    return s[start .. len(s)-1]            # empty string when start == len(s)

// Equivalent phrasing: take everything after the last ':' byte, then drop its first byte;
// error if there is nothing after the last ':' (i.e. the string's last byte is ':').

// ===== Specialised to this driver, where input = "Module::" + W =====
// len = 8 + len(W). "Module::" always supplies a ':' at index 7, so pos != -1 always.
//   if W is empty or W's LAST byte is ':'  -> last colon is at index len-1 -> start = len+1 > len -> CRASH
//   else if W contains ':' :
//        k = index (within W) of W's last ':' byte
//        result = W[k+2 ..]      (empty when k == len(W)-2)
//   else (no ':' in W):
//        pos = 7 (the second colon of "Module::"), start = 9 -> result = W[1..]  (W minus its FIRST BYTE)

// PORTING NOTE (Rust): must slice BYTES, e.g. &s.as_bytes()[start..], and produce a
// Vec<u8>/String::from_utf8_lossy-free byte string, because the result is frequently
// INVALID UTF-8 (see goldens for "é" and "日本語"). Using char_indices / &str[..] would panic.


CLAIMED FINDINGS:
1. CONFIRMED: demodulize(s) == s.substr(s.rfind(':') + 2). Every one of ~660 probes (20 hand-picked discriminators + 601 randomized words over the alphabet {a,b,':','::',':::',x,Y,_,space,-,'é',q} + non-ASCII + long strings) matched this model exactly, with zero mismatches in both value and crash/no-crash.
2. RULED OUT (a) pos=rfind("::"); substr(pos+3): discriminator W="a:" -> input "Module::a:" (len 10). rfind("::")=6 -> substr(9)="a:" (no crash). OBSERVED: crash with __pos 11 > size 10, i.e. pos+2 where pos=9=rfind(':'). Second discriminator W="a:bc" -> input "Module::a:bc" (len 12): rfind("::")=6 -> substr(9)="a:bc"; OBSERVED "c" = substr(11) = rfind(':')=9 plus 2.
3. RULED OUT (b) pos=find("::"); substr(pos+3) and (d) pos=find(':'); substr(pos+3): both always give find pos=6 -> substr(9), which for W="A::B" (input "Module::A::B", len 12) predicts "::B". OBSERVED: empty string. Also they would never crash for non-empty W, yet W="a:"/"a::"/":" all crash.
4. RULED OUT (e)-style two-step forms such as s.substr(pos+1).substr(1): the exception message names a single substr with __pos measured against the FULL string length (W="" -> "__pos (which is 9) > this->size() (which is 8)"; a two-step form would report __pos 1 > size 0). So it is one substr call on the whole string.
5. CONFIRMED (c): pos = rfind(':') (single byte 0x3A), return substr(pos + 2). Verified independently by the crash arithmetic: for every crashing input the message is exactly '__pos (which is N+1) > this->size() (which is N)' with N = 8 + byte_len(W) — consistent with last colon at index N-1 and start = N+1.
6. The search target is a SINGLE ':' byte, not the digraph "::": W="a:bc" -> "c" (last colon at input index 9, single, preceded by 'a').
7. Skip is a uniform +2 regardless of what precedes the last colon: W="a:bc" -> "c" and W="a::bc" -> "c" (last colon at 9 vs 10, both +2).
8. Byte comparison is exact/unsigned: W="\xba\xbab" (0xBA = 0x3A|0x80) -> result bytes ba 62, i.e. the 0xBA bytes were NOT treated as colons (pos stayed at 7 from the "Module::" prefix).
9. Other punctuation is not a separator: W="a;b" -> ";b", W="a.b" -> ".b", W="a/b" -> "/b", W="a|b" -> "|b" (all just input[9..], pos=7).
10. No case folding, trimming, or any other transformation: W="FooBar" -> "ooBar", W="HTTPServer" -> "TTPServer", W="no_colons_here" -> "o_colons_here", W="a::b " -> " " (trailing space preserved), W="a	b" -> "	b".
11. CRASH CONDITION (exact): std::out_of_range is thrown iff the LAST BYTE of the input string is ':' (equivalently, for this driver, iff W is empty or W's last byte is ':'). All other inputs return normally, possibly the empty string. Verified over 601 random inputs: crash <=> input ends with ':' held in every case.
12. Result is a raw BYTE slice with no UTF-8 awareness. W="é" (c3 a9) -> input "Module::" + c3 a9 (len 10), pos=7, substr(9) = single byte a9 = a lone UTF-8 continuation byte => INVALID UTF-8 output. W="日本語" (e6 97 a5 e6 9c ac e8 aa 9e) -> substr(9) = 97 a5 e6 9c ac e8 aa 9e, starts with continuation byte 0x97 => INVALID UTF-8. W="🎉" (f0 9f 8e 89) -> 9f 8e 89 => INVALID UTF-8. W="ü" (c3 bc) -> bc. W="€" (e2 82 ac) -> 82 ac.
13. W="café" -> "afé" (61 66 c3 a9) which happens to stay valid UTF-8 — so validity is incidental, purely a function of where byte 9 lands.
14. Length arithmetic is in bytes, confirmed via crash message: W="é:" (3 bytes) -> '__pos (which is 12) > this->size() (which is 11)' = 8+3=11. W="日本語:" (10 bytes) -> 19 > 18. W = 100*'z' + ':' (101 bytes) -> 110 > 109.
15. Long inputs behave identically (no truncation/limits): W = 500*'A' -> 499-byte result; W = "Mod::" + 300*'B' -> 299-byte result of all 'B' (last colon at index 12, substr(14)).
16. stdout produced before the throw IS flushed (std::endl flushes): crashing runs still emit the first 4 lines (pluralize, camelize, isPlural, isSingular) before aborting.
17. The 'no colon anywhere' case is unreachable through this driver because "Module::" is always prepended, so it cannot be observed. If the source literally is `s.substr(s.rfind(':') + 2)`, npos + 2 wraps to 1 and the C++ result would be s.substr(1) — which itself throws only for an empty s. A port only needs to be correct for inputs containing ':'.

CLAIMED UNCERTAINTIES:
The behavior when the input contains NO ':' at all is unobservable through this driver ("Module::" is always prepended). If the source is literally `s.substr(s.rfind(':') + 2)`, then npos+2 wraps to 1 and C++ would return s.substr(1) (throwing only for empty s). If instead there is a guard (`if (pos == npos) return s;`), the result would be s unchanged. I could not discriminate these. Recommendation for a port: only the has-colon path needs to be byte-exact; for the no-colon path pick a safe fallback (return the input unchanged) and document it, since no test can exercise it via this driver.
Cannot distinguish `rfind(':')` from `find_last_of(":")` / a manual reverse scan for byte 0x3A — they are behaviorally identical for a single-character needle, so this is a distinction without a difference.
Cannot distinguish `substr(pos + 2)` from `substr(pos + 1 + 1)` or from "take the suffix after the last colon then drop its first byte" — identical outputs AND identical crash set for all reachable inputs, except that the two-step form would report a different __pos in the exception text; the observed exception text matches the single-substr form, so the single-substr form is the one to port.
NUL bytes inside the string cannot be tested (execve/argv is NUL-terminated), so behavior for embedded 0x00 is unknown; a byte-faithful port will handle it naturally.
Whether the thrown exception type/message must be reproduced by a port is a policy question. A Rust port would presumably return Err/panic; the exact C++ stderr text and SIGABRT (status 134) are recorded in the goldens if byte-exact process behavior is required.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
